title: Memory Management: Fitting Programs into RAM

questions.question: What is the difference between a logical and a physical address?
options: Logical addresses are longer than physical ones
A logical address is what the program sees; the physical address is the real RAM location the MMU maps it to
Physical addresses exist only on disk
They are identical in every modern OS
questions.rationale: The program uses logical (virtual) addresses; the MMU translates each to a physical RAM location at run time, enabling isolation and relocation.

questions.question: Free memory exists but is scattered into small, non-contiguous holes that cannot satisfy a request. This is called:
questions.rationale: External fragmentation is free memory broken into scattered holes; its cures are compaction (shuffling processes together) or paging.

questions.question: Why does paging eliminate external fragmentation?
options: Because every page must be physically adjacent to its neighbours
Because any page can be placed in any free frame of the same size
Because pages are always contiguous on disk
Because the TLB merges holes automatically
questions.rationale: Paging divides memory into fixed-size pages and frames, and any page can occupy any free frame — so no unusable gaps remain between allocations.

questions.question: With a 20 ns TLB lookup, 100 ns memory access, and an 80% TLB hit ratio, what is the effective access time?
questions.rationale: Hit cost = 20 + 100 = 120 ns; miss cost = 20 + 100 + 100 = 220 ns; effective time = 0.8 × 120 + 0.2 × 220 = 140 ns.

questions.question: What is the final step when servicing a page fault?
options: Restart the faulting instruction so the process never notices
questions.rationale: After loading the page and updating the page table, the OS restarts the faulting instruction — the transparent restart is what makes demand paging work.

questions.question: Belady's anomaly, where adding frames increases page faults, afflicts which replacement algorithm?
questions.rationale: FIFO can produce more faults with 4 frames (10) than with 3 (9) on the same reference string; LRU and Optimal are immune to the anomaly.

questions.question: On the reference string 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5 with 3 frames, how many faults do FIFO, LRU, and Optimal produce respectively?
questions.rationale: The classic result is FIFO = 9, LRU = 10, and Optimal = 7 faults; Optimal is unimplementable and serves only as a benchmark.

questions.question: A system where processes fault continuously and the CPU is busy servicing faults instead of executing is:
questions.rationale: Thrashing is the death spiral from too few frames per process; throughput collapses even though the CPU appears 100% busy.

questions.question: The working set of a process is:
options: All pages the process will ever use
The set of pages used in the last Δ references — the memory it truly needs
The pages currently on the swap disk
One page of the page table
questions.rationale: The working-set model counts pages used in a recent window Δ; guaranteeing each process its working set is the cure for thrashing.

questions.question: How does segmentation differ from paging?
options: Segments are fixed-size units of physical memory
Segments are variable-size and divided by meaning (code, stack, heap), while paging divides by size
Segmentation cannot be combined with paging
Segmentation removes internal fragmentation but causes page faults
questions.rationale: Segmentation divides memory by logical meaning into variable-size segments; paging divides by size. Real systems like x86 combine both — segment logically, then page each segment.
